research.topic: Move VM transaction atomicity — how Aptos/Sui guarantee an aborted transaction writes nothing but gas, and the exact staged-session pattern AINCORE must adopt given that `coin::deduct_gas` must survive a user abort (BLOCKER-1)

sources.title: move-vm Session (LOCAL, the exact version AINCORE links)
sources.key_takeaway: `Session { runtime, data_cache, native_extensions }` (:29-33). `finish(self)` (:241) CONSUMES the session and calls `data_cache.into_effects()`. There is no `abort()`, no snapshot, no undo. The doc comments say the caller must not proceed with effect generation after a violation — the adapter contract is: to discard, you DROP the Session and never call finish(). Dropping is a real, complete rollback because the Session OWNS the TransactionDataCache.

sources.title: move-vm TransactionDataCache (LOCAL)
sources.key_takeaway: `into_effects` (:75-138) walks `account_map` and emits an Op for EVERY GlobalValue whose `into_effect()` is Some — it has no concept of 'which action wrote this' and no success flag. Module publishes are staged in `module_map` and emitted as Op::New/Op::Modify identically (:79-85). Confirms the audit: session.finish() after an abort returns the partial writes verbatim. `new(remote, loader)` (:62) takes any `&'r S: MoveResolver` — this is the seam an overlay resolver plugs into.

sources.title: move-vm GlobalValue state machine (LOCAL)
sources.key_takeaway: `GlobalValueImpl` = None | Fresh | Cached{status} | Deleted (:186-198). `mark_dirty()` (:279) is called from the WRITE paths (:767, :831, :2035, :2109, :2141) — i.e. at the moment of mutation, not at commit. `into_effect` (:2524-2538): Fresh→Op::New unconditionally, Deleted→Op::Delete, Cached+Dirty→Op::Modify, Cached+Clean→None. `move_to` on a Deleted slot goes straight to Cached{Dirty} (:2499). Nothing anywhere restores a Dirty back to Clean. Rollback is structurally impossible inside one session.

sources.title: move-vm MoveVM::new_session (LOCAL)
sources.key_takeaway: `pub fn new_session<'r, S: MoveResolver>(&self, remote: &'r S) -> Session<'r,'_,S>` — sessions are cheap and can be created repeatedly against DIFFERENT resolvers on the same MoveVM. Also exposes `flush_loader_cache_if_invalidated()` (:102), needed between staged sessions when a stage published modules.

sources.title: aptos-core: AptosVM::execute_user_transaction_impl
sources.key_takeaway: The canonical three-stage flow: `PrologueSession::new(...)` → `prologue_session.execute(|s| self.validate_signed_transaction(...))` wrapped in `unwrap_or_discard!` → `prologue_session.into_user_session(...)` returns `(SystemSessionChangeSet, UserSession)` → payload runs in the UserSession → on Err, `on_user_transaction_execution_failure(prologue_change_set, err, ...)`. The prologue change set is a SEPARATE, TYPED value carried past the failure point; the user session's change set is simply never produced.

sources.title: aptos-core: failed_transaction_cleanup + finish_aborted_transaction
sources.key_takeaway: Verbatim comment at :663-668: "The transaction should be kept. Run the appropriate post transaction workflows including epilogue. This runs a new session that ignores any side effects that might abort the execution (e.g., spending additional funds needed to pay for gas)." `finish_aborted_transaction` takes ONLY `prologue_session_change_set`, then `EpilogueSession::on_user_session_failure(self, txn_data, resolver, previous_session_change_set)` (:861) and `run_failure_epilogue(session, ..., gas_meter.balance(), fee_statement, ...)`. `const ZERO_STORAGE_REFUND: u64 = 0; // Storage refund is zero since no slots are deleted in aborted transactions.` The same `gas_meter` object is threaded through all three stages, so gas burned by the aborted payload is still charged.

sources.title: aptos-core: multisig inner-payload discard (the closest analogue to AINCORE's must_succeed pre-action)
sources.key_takeaway: Verbatim: "Step 2: Execute the target payload. Transaction failure here is tolerated. In case of any failures, we'll discard the session and start a new one. This ensures that any data changes are not persisted." And in `failure_multisig_payload_cleanup`: "Start a fresh session for running cleanup that does not contain any changes from the inner function call earlier (since it failed)." The cleanup call runs with `&mut UnmeteredGasMeter`. This is exactly AINCORE's shape: an outer stage whose writes MUST survive an inner stage that MAY abort.

sources.title: aptos-core: RespawnedSession + PrologueSession/UserSession/EpilogueSession/AbortHookSession
sources.key_takeaway: All four session types are `#[derive(Deref, DerefMut)] struct X<'r> { session: RespawnedSession<'r> }`. `RespawnedSession::spawn` builds an `ExecutorViewWithChangeSet` over the raw base view, wraps it in a `StorageAdapter` resolver via `vm.as_move_resolver_with_group_view(executor_view)`, and creates a NEW MoveVM session on it (self-referential borrow). `finish_with_squashed_change_set` merges the new session's change set into the one already in the executor view. Doc comment: "We finish the session after the user transaction is done running to get the change set and charge gas and storage fee based on it before running storage refunds and the transaction epilogue." This is the mechanism that lets stage N+1 SEE stage N's writes without stage N's writes being inside a session that could be discarded.

sources.title: aptos-core: ExecutorViewWithChangeSet (the overlay resolver)
sources.key_takeaway: "Adapter to allow resolving the calls to `ExecutorView` via change set." Reads check `self.change_set.resource_write_set().get(state_key)` FIRST and fall through to the base view only on miss (:73-101, :246-300). Deletions in the change set resolve to `Ok(None)` — they are NOT a miss. This is the whole trick, and it is ~60 lines.

sources.title: aptos-core: charge_change_set / charge_change_set_and_respawn_session
sources.key_takeaway: IO/storage gas is charged by ITERATING the finished change set (`for (key, op_size) in change_set.write_set_size_iter() { gas_meter.charge_io_gas_for_write(...) }`) AFTER the user session finishes, then the epilogue is respawned on top. On the failure path this iteration runs over the abort-hook/prologue change set only — the discarded user writes are never priced and never written.

sources.title: Sui: GasCharger::reset + TemporaryStore::drop_writes
sources.key_takeaway: Sui's equivalent is explicit and blunt: `pub fn reset(&mut self, temporary_store) { temporary_store.drop_writes(); self.gas_status.reset_storage_cost_and_rebate(); self.smash_gas(temporary_store); }` — "Resets any mutations, deletions, and events recorded in the store... Effects on store are now as if we were about to begin execution." In `legacy_charge_gas`: "On error we need to dump writes, deletes, etc before charging storage gas" → `if execution_result.is_err() { self.reset(temporary_store); }`, then `ensure_active_inputs_mutated()` + `collect_storage_and_rebate()` re-derive the gas-only effects. Note `drop_writes` also clears events.

sources.title: Sui: execution_engine.rs error path
sources.key_takeaway: Gas is smashed/reserved BEFORE the PTB runs; on any command failure the whole PTB's writes are dumped and only gas effects survive. Post-reset the engine re-runs `check_conservation_invariants` and treats a violation after reset as fatal — i.e. the discard path is itself invariant-checked, not trusted.

sources.title: AINCORE: the two files that must change
sources.key_takeaway: AINCORE is unusually well-positioned: `AINCOREStorage` implements only `ModuleResolver::get_module` and `ResourceResolver::get_resource` over flat string keys `module_{addr}_{name}` / `resource_{addr}_{tag}`, and `changeset_to_kv` already emits exactly those keys as `Vec<(String, Option<String>)>`. An overlay resolver is therefore a ~40-line struct, and change-set squash is plain per-key last-write-wins (no aggregators, no delayed fields, no resource groups — the parts that make Aptos's version complicated do not exist here).

research.how_reference_impls_do_it:
MECHANISM ESTABLISHED FROM THE LOCAL VM SOURCE (part a)

The Move VM has exactly one rollback primitive and it is not a function call — it is `drop`. `Session` (session.rs:29-33) owns its `TransactionDataCache`; `finish(self)` (session.rs:241) consumes the session and calls `data_cache.into_effects()`. `into_effects` (data_cache.rs:75-138) iterates `account_map` and emits an Op for every `GlobalValue` whose `into_effect()` is `Some`, plus every entry in `module_map`. It has no success flag and no provenance — it cannot tell you which action produced which Op. `GlobalValueImpl::into_effect` (values_impl.rs:2524-2538) maps Fresh→Op::New unconditionally, Deleted→Op::Delete, Cached{Dirty}→Op::Modify, Cached{Clean}→None. `mark_dirty()` is invoked from the mutation paths themselves (values_impl.rs:767, 831, 2035, 2109, 2141), i.e. at the instruction that writes, and nothing anywhere flips Dirty back to Clean. Therefore: (1) AINCORE's audit finding is exactly right — after an abort, `finish()` returns the partial writes; (2) there is no filter you can apply to the returned ChangeSet to remove "the aborted action's writes", because the ChangeSet does not record which action wrote what; (3) the ONLY correct discard is to never call `finish()` and let the `Session` drop, which frees the whole `account_map` and is a complete rollback.

The seam that makes staging possible: `MoveVM::new_session<'r, S: MoveResolver>(&self, remote: &'r S)` (move_vm.rs:55) accepts ANY resolver. Sessions are cheap and repeatable on one `MoveVM`.

HOW APTOS DOES IT (part b)

Aptos never puts writes that must survive and writes that may be discarded into the same session. `aptos-move/aptos-vm/src/aptos_vm.rs::execute_user_transaction_impl` (~line 2138) runs three (sometimes four) distinct sessions:

1. `PrologueSession::new(self, &txn_data, resolver)`, then `prologue_session.execute(|session| self.validate_signed_transaction(...))` wrapped in `unwrap_or_discard!`. The prologue does signature/AA validation, sequence-number increment, and the max-gas withdrawal. If the prologue itself fails the transaction is DISCARDED entirely (no writes, not even the sequence bump). Then `prologue_session.into_user_session(self, &txn_data, resolver, change_set_configs, code_storage)` returns `(SystemSessionChangeSet, UserSession<'r>)` — the prologue's writes are extracted into an owned, typed change-set value and the prologue session is consumed.

2. `UserSession` is a `RespawnedSession` spawned over the prologue change set: `RespawnedSession::spawn` constructs an `ExecutorViewWithChangeSet` layering the prologue change set over the raw base view, wraps it in a resolver (`vm.as_move_resolver_with_group_view(executor_view)`), and creates a brand-new MoveVM session on that resolver. The user payload runs here. On success, `UserSession::finish` → `finish_with_squashed_change_set` merges user writes onto the prologue change set. On failure, the `UserSession` is simply dropped and its change set is never produced.

3. Failure path: `on_user_transaction_execution_failure` → `failed_transaction_cleanup(prologue_session_change_set, error_vm_status, gas_meter, ...)` (aptos_vm.rs:620). If the status is `Keep`, it calls `finish_aborted_transaction(prologue_session_change_set, gas_meter, ...)` (aptos_vm.rs:757) — note the signature takes the PROLOGUE change set and nothing else. Verbatim comment at :663-668: "This runs a new session that ignores any side effects that might abort the execution (e.g., spending additional funds needed to pay for gas)." It sets `const ZERO_STORAGE_REFUND: u64 = 0; // Storage refund is zero since no slots are deleted in aborted transactions`, optionally runs an `AbortHookSession` (lazy account creation, retried with `&mut UnmeteredGasMeter` if it OOGs), then `EpilogueSession::on_user_session_failure(self, txn_data, resolver, previous_session_change_set)` (:861) and `run_failure_epilogue(session, module_storage, serialized_signers, gas_meter.balance(), fee_statement, ...)`. The epilogue is again a respawned session over the prologue-only change set — it CANNOT see the aborted user writes because they were never put into any resolver.

Gas on a failed transaction: the SAME `&mut impl AptosGasMeter` is threaded through prologue → user → epilogue, so execution gas burned by the aborting payload is still counted. `fee_statement_from_gas_meter(txn_data, gas_meter, ZERO_STORAGE_REFUND)` derives the charge from `max_gas_amount - gas_meter.balance()`, and the epilogue Move function does the actual balance mutation. IO/storage gas is charged by iterating the FINISHED change set — `charge_change_set` (aptos_vm.rs:1213): `for (key, op_size) in change_set.write_set_size_iter() { gas_meter.charge_io_gas_for_write(key, &op_size)?; }` — so on the abort path only the surviving (prologue/abort-hook) writes are priced. `charge_change_set_and_respawn_session` (:1243) is the success-path twin: charge from the user change set, then `EpilogueSession::on_user_session_success(...)`.

The multisig path is the exact analogue of AINCORE's must_succeed-pre-action-plus-fallible-payload problem, and Aptos states the rule in comments: "Step 2: Execute the target payload. Transaction failure here is tolerated. In case of any failures, we'll discard the session and start a new one. This ensures that any data changes are not persisted." and, in `failure_multisig_payload_cleanup` (:1519), "Start a fresh session for running cleanup that does not contain any changes from the inner function call earlier (since it failed)." The cleanup Move call there runs with `&mut UnmeteredGasMeter`.

`ExecutorViewWithChangeSet` (view_with_change_set.rs) is the whole overlay: reads consult `change_set.resource_write_set().get(state_key)` first and fall through to the base view only on a miss; a `WriteOp::Deletion` in the change set resolves to `Ok(None)` rather than falling through.

HOW SUI DOES IT

Sui uses a mutable `TemporaryStore` plus an explicit dump instead of session layering. `GasCharger::reset` (gas_charger.rs:312): `temporary_store.drop_writes(); self.gas_status.reset_storage_cost_and_rebate(); self.smash_gas(temporary_store);` — documented as "Resets any mutations, deletions, and events recorded in the store, as well as any storage costs and rebates, then re-runs gas smashing. Effects on store are now as if we were about to begin execution." In `legacy_charge_gas`: "On error we need to dump writes, deletes, etc before charging storage gas" → `if execution_result.is_err() { self.reset(temporary_store); }`, then `ensure_active_inputs_mutated()` + `collect_storage_and_rebate(self)` re-derive the gas-only effects, and `temporary_store.into_effects(...)` produces the final effects. Gas is reserved from the gas coin BEFORE execution and refunded after, so the charge survives the dump. `drop_writes` also clears accumulator events. Sui then re-runs `check_conservation_invariants` AFTER the reset and treats a post-reset violation as fatal — the discard path is itself verified, not trusted.

DIEM ORIGIN

Both designs descend from Diem's `MoveVM` adapter split of `prologue` / `transaction payload` / `epilogue` as three separate VM invocations against a shared `TransactionDataCache`-per-stage, with the prologue charging the max gas deposit and the epilogue refunding the unused remainder — the reason the split exists at all is precisely AINCORE's constraint: the fee must be collected even when the payload aborts.
research.pitfalls:
1. FILTERING THE CHANGESET INSTEAD OF SPLITTING SESSIONS. The most tempting wrong fix: call `session.finish()`, then drop entries "belonging to" the aborted action. `into_effects` (data_cache.rs:75-138) has no provenance whatsoever — it emits one Op per (address, type) slot regardless of which action dirtied it. If the prologue and the payload both touch the sender's CoinStore (they do — `deduct_gas` writes it, `coin::transfer` writes it), the two writes are the SAME `GlobalValue` and are indistinguishable in the output. Filtering is not merely fragile, it is impossible. Separate `Session` objects are mandatory.

2. RE-RUNNING THE PROLOGUE INSTEAD OF LAYERING IT. Second tempting wrong fix: drop everything on abort, then open a fresh session and re-run `deduct_gas`. This double-charges execution gas unless the meter is carefully reset, doubles VM work on the abort path (a cheap DoS amplifier — attacker submits guaranteed-aborting txs), and re-reads state that may have been mutated by the discarded session's native extensions. Aptos never re-runs; it layers via `ExecutorViewWithChangeSet`. Do the same.

3. THE OVERLAY TREATING A STAGED DELETE AS A MISS. `overlay.get(k).unwrap_or_else(|| base.get(k))` resurrects deleted resources: stage 1 deletes `resource_X`, stage 2 reads it, gets the stale DB value, and the resource is alive again. `ExecutorViewWithChangeSet` matches deletions explicitly to `Ok(None)`. In the sketch above this is the `Some(None) => Ok(None)` arm — it is the single most likely line to get wrong and it is silently exploitable (e.g. an unbonding entry deleted in one stage and observed live in the next — the same shape as BLOCKER-2's exploit).

4. FORGETTING MODULES IN THE OVERLAY. `DataStore::exists_module` (data_cache.rs:274-287) and `load_module` (:234) both fall through to `remote.get_module`. If the overlay only covers resources, a module published in stage 1 is invisible in stage 2 (LINKER_ERROR) or, worse, a stage-1 module upgrade is silently ignored while the `Loader` serves the old code. Cover `get_module` in the overlay AND call `MoveVM::flush_loader_cache_if_invalidated()` (move_vm.rs:102) between stages when the prior stage published — the `Loader` cache lives on the `MoveVM`, not the `Session`, so it survives the stage boundary and is the one piece of state that layering does NOT isolate.

5. A METERED EPILOGUE. If stage 3 runs on the shared, nearly-exhausted `gas_meter`, an abort that consumed the full limit makes the fee/refund write itself run out of gas and vanish — aborts become free again, which is the exact spam vector the whole design is protecting. Aptos uses `&mut UnmeteredGasMeter` in `failure_multisig_payload_cleanup` and retries the abort-hook unmetered ("If this fails, it is likely due to out of gas, so we try again without metering and then validate below that we charged sufficiently"). Note the second half of that comment: after running unmetered they VERIFY the charge covered the cost. Do both — unmetered epilogue plus an assertion that the fee actually landed.

6. A PROLOGUE FAILURE THAT "KEEPS PARTIAL PROLOGUE WRITES". If stage 1 has several must_succeed actions and action 2 fails after action 1 wrote, keeping action 1's writes recreates BLOCKER-1 one level up. Aptos's `unwrap_or_discard!` discards the ENTIRE transaction (not even the sequence bump) on prologue failure. Stage 1 must be all-or-nothing: propagate with `?` and let the caller emit a discard, never a partial commit. A discarded transaction must also not be counted as executed for nonce purposes.

7. EVENTS. `into_effects` returns `(ChangeSet, Vec<Event>)` and AINCORE currently discards events (`let (changeset, _events)`). When events are eventually wired to the API/indexer, the aborted stage's events must be dropped with its writes — Sui's `drop_writes` explicitly clears accumulator events, and an event stream that reports an abort's effects as real is an oracle/indexer poisoning vector. Wire events per-stage from the start so this cannot be forgotten.

8. NON-DETERMINISM SNEAKING INTO THE STAGING ORDER. The squash must be a fixed sequence (prologue → user → epilogue) with per-key last-write-wins. `into_effects` uses BTreeMaps so each stage is internally deterministic; keep `staged` a BTreeMap and emit `into_iter()` order. Do not build the final Vec by concatenating stage Vecs in a HashMap-derived order, and do not sort by tx_hash at this layer.

9. PARTIAL-ABORT SEMANTICS. The sketch breaks out of the user loop on the first abort. If instead you continue executing later user actions after one aborts, you are back to "some user writes committed, some not" — a different flavour of the same bug, and it makes the `status` field meaningless. One abort = the entire user stage is discarded.

10. LIFETIMES. `Session<'r,'l,S>` borrows the resolver, so a naive `struct StagedSession { overlay: OverlayStorage, session: Session<'_,'_,_> }` is self-referential and will not compile (this is why Aptos's `RespawnedSession` needs the ouroboros-style construction). AINCORE does not need that: construct the overlay as a plain local, create the session in the same block, and let only the owned `Vec`/`BTreeMap` of writes escape the scope. Any attempt to return the session from a helper function will fight the borrow checker — keep each stage inline or return the change set, never the session.

11. DON'T LET THIS FIX MASK BLOCKER-2. Once sessions are staged, every transaction writes the sender's CoinStore (deduct_gas) and possibly a fee destination. Those keys must be in `analyze_tx`'s declared conflict set at core/executor/src/lib.rs (~2174-2330) or the parallel scheduler will co-batch transactions that now genuinely conflict, and the last-write-wins commit loop will erase gas deductions — turning a correctness fix into a new free-execution vector. Fix the two together, and prefer deriving deps from the real key set over extending the hand-written per-module lists.

research.topic: Parallel-execution conflict detection for AINCORE: replacing hand-written per-module dependency sets (executor::analyze_tx) with a sound mechanism — evaluated against Block-STM/Aptos, Sui's declared-object model, and Move's own `acquires` + the read-write-set static analyzer that ships in the local move checkout

sources.title: Block-STM: Scaling Blockchain Execution by Turning Ordering Curse to a Performance Blessing (arXiv 2203.06871, PPoPP'23)
sources.key_takeaway: Block-STM requires NO a-priori read/write sets. It executes optimistically against an MVMemory (multi-version map location -> (txn_idx, incarnation) -> value), RECORDS the read set during execution, then a validation task re-checks that recorded read set against MVMemory for writes by lower-index txs. Failure -> abort, bump incarnation, re-execute. Aborted incarnations' writes are marked ESTIMATE so later readers suspend instead of reading stale data. Determinism comes from committing in the preset block order, not from the scheduler. Two atomics (execution_idx, validation_idx) drive a collaborative scheduler. The central lesson for AINCORE: the read/write set is an OUTPUT of execution, and safety comes from validating it after the fact — never from a declaration written by hand before the fact.

sources.title: Sui object model, object ownership, and shared-object version assignment
sources.key_takeaway: Sui's up-front declaration is sound for a LANGUAGE reason, not a scheduler reason: Sui Move has no borrow_global — every object a tx touches MUST be passed in as an argument (ObjectArg::ImmOrOwnedObject{id,version,digest} or ObjectArg::SharedObject{id,initial_shared_version,mutable}), and the runtime rejects any access to an undeclared object. Owned objects are version-locked per validator so they skip consensus entirely; shared objects get a consensus-assigned version (Lamport: new version = 1 + max(input versions)) and then execute in parallel across disjoint object sets. AINCORE uses CORE Move with ambient borrow_global_mut, so this soundness argument does NOT transfer — the same up-front-declaration idea in core Move is unenforceable, which is exactly why analyze_tx is broken.

sources.title: Move bytecode acquires verifier — LOCAL SOURCE (definitive answer to 'is acquires usable?')
sources.key_takeaway: acquires IS in the compiled binary: FunctionDefinition.acquires_global_resources: Vec<StructDefinitionIndex>. But it is UNSOUND as a write-set source for three proven reasons: (a) function_acquired_resources returns BTreeSet::new() when function_handle.module != self_handle_idx — acquires is transitive INTRA-module only, never across modules; (b) MoveTo/MoveToGeneric and Exists are in the verifier's explicit no-op arm, so resource CREATION is invisible in acquires; (c) StructDefinitionIndex is type-level with no address, while AINCORE's conflict tokens are resource_{addr}_{StructTag}. Fact (a) IS blocker-2 verbatim: governance.move:45 create_proposal declares `acquires GovernanceState` yet governance.move:52 calls staking::burn_ain, which is `acquires ValidatorSet, SupplyStats` (staking.move:528) — identical pattern at token_factory.move:87.

research.how_reference_impls_do_it:
CAN `acquires` GIVE US A TRANSITIVE RESOURCE SET? — Definitive answer from the local source: NO, and it is not a close call.

`acquires` is in the compiled binary (`FunctionDefinition.acquires_global_resources: Vec<StructDefinitionIndex>`, move-binary-format/src/file_format.rs:477), and inside a single module it IS transitive — `AcquiresVerifier::call_acquire` forces a caller to declare everything its callee acquires. But `function_acquired_resources` (acquires_list_verifier.rs ~line 213) opens with:

    if function_handle.module != self.module.self_handle_idx() { return BTreeSet::new(); }

Cross-module calls contribute NOTHING. That single line is blocker-2's root cause expressed in the compiler: `governance::create_proposal` (governance.move:45) declares `acquires GovernanceState` and nothing else, while governance.move:52 calls `staking::burn_ain`, declared `acquires ValidatorSet, SupplyStats` at staking.move:528. Same at token_factory.move:87. So the *language itself* already lost the information that analyze_tx is missing — you cannot recover it by reading acquires; you would have to rebuild the cross-module call graph yourself from FunctionHandles and take the closure, which is 80% of writing a static analyzer. Two further disqualifiers: `MoveTo`/`MoveToGeneric` and `Exists` sit in the verifier's explicit no-op match arm, so resource CREATION never appears in acquires (coin::register's `move_to<CoinStore>` is invisible); and `StructDefinitionIndex` is type-level with no address, whereas AINCORE tokens are `resource_{addr}_{StructTag}` — acquires can tell you "some CoinStore", never "0xABC's CoinStore".

HOW THE REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATIONS ACTUALLY SOLVE IT:

Block-STM / Aptos — declare nothing, validate everything. Each tx executes optimistically against MVMemory (an MVHashMap: location -> BTreeMap<txn_idx, (incarnation, value)>), and the runtime RECORDS the read set as a side effect of execution (`CapturedReads`). A separate validation task then re-checks that recorded read set against MVMemory; if any lower-index tx has since written a location the tx read, the incarnation is aborted, its writes in MVMemory are flagged ESTIMATE (so a later reader suspends and waits rather than reading a doomed value), and the tx is re-executed with incarnation+1. Two atomics (execution_idx, validation_idx) drive a collaborative scheduler where any thread can pick up execution or validation work; `decrease_cnt` handles the re-validation wave after an abort. The output is byte-identical to sequential execution in the preset block order, which is what makes it consensus-safe. Two operational details Aptos needed and AINCORE will need too: (i) `BlockExecutor` FALLS BACK TO SEQUENTIAL on speculative errors and module publishes rather than guessing; (ii) AggregatorV2 / delayed fields (mvhashmap/src/versioned_delayed_fields.rs) exist specifically because a single hot counter — total supply — otherwise conflicts with every tx and collapses parallelism to 1.

Sui — declare everything up front, but the LANGUAGE enforces it. Sui Move has no `borrow_global`. Every object a tx touches must be passed as an argument: `ObjectArg::ImmOrOwnedObject((id, version, digest))` or `ObjectArg::SharedObject { id, initial_shared_version, mutable }`, and the runtime rejects any access to an object not in the declared input set. Owned objects are version-locked per validator, so owned-only txs skip consensus entirely; shared objects get a consensus-assigned version via a Lamport rule (new version = 1 + max(input versions)), after which txs with disjoint object sets execute in parallel. The soundness argument is "the VM cannot reach undeclared state", not "the scheduler is clever". This is precisely why the same pattern is unsound in AINCORE: core Move's ambient `borrow_global_mut` means a declared input set is a promise the VM never checks.

Move's own answer, sitting in the local checkout — `language/tools/read-write-set`. Diem built exactly the option-(3) analyzer, for exactly this purpose. `read_write_set::analyze(modules)` computes the module dependency graph, topologically sorts it, and runs the move-prover stackless-bytecode `ReadWriteSetProcessor` over the whole program — genuinely cross-module transitive, which is what acquires refuses to be. `.normalize_all_scripts(add_ons)` yields a `NormalizedReadWriteSetAnalysis` you cache; per tx you then call `get_keys_written(module, fun, signers, actuals, type_actuals, blockchain_view) -> Result<Vec<ResourceKey>>` (and `get_keys_read`). `ResourceKey { address, type_ }` maps 1:1 onto `resource_{addr}_{StructTag}`. Access paths carry an `Access` enum (Read / Write / ReadWrite) so read-read pairs need not conflict. It over-approximates (the safe direction), and its two failure modes are explicit and checkable: `may_have_secondary_indexes(module, fun) -> Result<bool>`, and `concretize_secondary_indexes` returns `Option` — `None`/`Err` must mean "serialize this tx", never "assume empty".
research.applicable_pattern:
FIRST, A CORRECTION TO THE FRAMING. Option (1) — "default-deny / conservative serialization for any tx touching an unmodelled 0x1 module" — is ALREADY SHIPPED in AINCORE. `analyze_tx` returns `(Vec<String>, bool)` where the bool is `recognized`, and `schedule_batches` (core/executor/src/lib.rs:2364-2377) flushes the current batch, clears the lock set, and runs any `!recognized` tx as a singleton. Modules genuinely absent from the match — epoch, universal_mining, wbtc, treasury, scripts, and every coin:: function other than transfer — are already fully serialized and are NOT the bug. Blocker-2 is the opposite failure: governance and token_factory set `recognized = true` and then under-declare. The safety boundary is not "unmodelled module"; it is "modelled module whose declared token set is not a superset of its true write set". Any plan built on option (1) as stated will produce a no-op patch.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE — three layers, safety first, performance last. This mirrors Aptos: correctness from validation, speed from analysis, and analysis never load-bearing for safety.

LAYER 0 — stop the bleeding (hours, ~40 lines, ship this on the audit branch now).
Two parts, and the second is the one that matters.
(a) In `analyze_tx`, every branch that can transitively reach `staking::burn_ain` must push `validator_set_key()` and `format!("resource_{}_0x1::staking::SupplyStats", system_address())`. Today that is the governance branch (:2276-2300) and both token_factory branches (:2288, :2307-2322). This closes the proven withdraw_unbonded-vs-token_factory mint.
(b) Add a `#[test]` that loads the compiled stdlib blobs, walks the cross-module call graph from every function named in `analyze_tx`'s match, unions each callee's `acquires_global_resources` resolved to `StructTag`s, and asserts the result is covered by the tokens that branch declares. This is the durable artifact — it converts "someone remembered" into "CI fails". Note it must walk the call graph itself precisely because `acquires` stops at module boundaries; treat `acquires` as a per-function local fact and do the closure in Rust. Add `move_to` targets by scanning `Bytecode::MoveTo/MoveToGeneric` operands, since acquires omits them.

LAYER 1 — the actual fix: optimistic execution with post-batch write-set validation (days, ~150 lines). This is Block-STM's safety property without Block-STM's machinery, and it fits AINCORE's existing shape almost exactly.
The pieces are already there: `execute_transaction` returns `Option<(Vec<(String, Option<String>)>, u128)>` — the tx's full WRITE set, by key. What's missing is the READ set. Get it by wrapping the resolver/`DataStore` that vm_move hands the Move session in a recording adapter that logs every `get_resource`/`get_module` key into a `Mutex<HashSet<String>>` (one small struct; the same wrapper is also where you'd later hang MVMemory if you go full Block-STM). Then in the batch loop at lib.rs:1582:
  1. `par_iter()` the batch as today, but each result now carries (write_keys, read_keys).
  2. Before building the WriteBatch, in the deterministic tx_hash sort order, sweep for conflicts: tx j conflicts with an earlier tx i if `write(i) ∩ (read(j) ∪ write(j)) != ∅`.
  3. If no conflict, commit exactly as today — zero behaviour change, zero perf cost on the happy path.
  4. If conflict, DISCARD the whole batch's results and re-run the conflicting suffix strictly sequentially (each tx sees the committed state of its predecessors). Simplest correct version: re-run the entire batch sequentially.
This makes `analyze_tx` a pure performance hint that can be wrong without being dangerous — which is the property you actually want, and the property Sui gets from its language and Aptos gets from validation. It also fixes the `sys:total_supply` mirror corruption at lib.rs:975-1010 for free, since that key lands in the write set like any other.
Do NOT ship the cheap shortcut of "treat write set as read set and skip the recording resolver". It catches write-write but misses read-then-write-elsewhere — e.g. a tx that reads `ValidatorSet.total_supply` and writes only a CoinStore, racing a tx that writes ValidatorSet. That is a live mint shape in this codebase.

LAYER 2 — restore parallelism with real static analysis (weeks, once Layer 1 makes it non-load-bearing).
Add `read-write-set` as a git dep at the pinned rev (`move-language/move`, branch aptos-v1.3.0 — same checkout AINCORE already uses per core/vm_move/Cargo.toml:8-20). At node start, and again after any successful `PublishModule`, build `NormalizedReadWriteSetAnalysis` over the loaded module set and cache it behind an `ArcSwap`. Replace the hand-written match in `analyze_tx` with:
    match rws.get_keys_written(&call.module, &call.function, &[sender], &call.args, &call.ty_args, &resolver) {
        Ok(keys) => tokens from keys (+ get_keys_read for the read side), recognized = true,
        Err(_) => recognized = false,   // serialize
    }
and force `recognized = false` whenever `may_have_secondary_indexes(module, fun)` is true and concretization fails. Cost is paid once per module-set change, not per tx. Keep Layer 1's validation switched on permanently: the analysis is an over-approximation and may still be wrong about AINCORE-specific patterns, and you now have a cheap runtime check that says so instead of forking the chain.

HOT-KEY NOTE, applies to all layers. `staking::ValidatorSet` at @0x1 is a single blob holding `total_supply` alongside the validator list, and `burn_ain` mutates it. Once conflict detection is CORRECT, every tx that burns anything — governance proposals, token_factory creates, fee burns, staking ops — serializes against every other. That is safe but it is roughly "no parallelism for system txs". Aptos hit exactly this and answered it with AggregatorV2 delayed fields (commutative +/- with bounds, resolved at commit). The AINCORE-shaped version is to split the monotone counters (`total_supply`, `cumulative_burned`) out of `ValidatorSet` into their own resource and give the executor a commutative-delta merge for those two keys, instead of last-write-wins. Do that only after Layer 1 lands, and treat it as an economics-sensitive change — it touches the supply cap tripwire.
research.pitfalls:
1. ORDERING VS BLOCKER-1 — this is the one that will bite. Any validate-and-re-execute scheme rests on Block-STM's assumption that re-executing a tx from a given state yields the same output. With BLOCKER-1 unfixed, an aborted tx still commits partial writes, and WHICH partial writes depends on where execution stopped — which depends on gas and on the state it read. Re-run the same tx after a different predecessor and you get a different write set, so validation can loop or, worse, commit a set that no sequential execution would produce. Fix BLOCKER-1 first; Layer 1 is unsound before it, not merely incomplete. Same coupling in the other direction: any "drop the session on abort" fix must preserve the `coin::deduct_gas` pre-action commit (must_succeed=true, lib.rs:2667-2693) or aborts become free and the optimistic executor becomes a free re-execution DoS.

2. THE NO-OP PATCH. As above: adding more "unmodelled module -> serialize" logic changes nothing, because that already exists and the broken branches are the RECOGNIZED ones. If a fix lands and blocker-2's PoC still mints, this is why.

3. `acquires` USED NAIVELY IS A FALSE SENSE OF SAFETY. Reading `acquires_global_resources` off compiled bytecode and calling it a write set produces a set that (a) silently drops every cross-module effect — i.e. drops precisely `staking::burn_ain`, i.e. reproduces blocker-2 while looking rigorous; (b) omits every `move_to` (resource creation, e.g. coin::register minting a CoinStore); (c) carries no address, so it cannot generate `resource_{addr}_{StructTag}` tokens without a separate story for where the address comes from. If someone proposes "derive deps from acquires", the answer is that Move's own verifier explicitly refuses to make it transitive.

4. OVER-APPROXIMATION SILENTLY BECOMING UNDER-APPROXIMATION. `read-write-set` is sound only when concretization succeeds. `get_keys_written` returns `Result`, `get_keys_read` returns `Result`, `concretize_secondary_indexes` returns `Option`, and `get_keys_written`/`get_keys_read` internally `ok_or_else(...)` on a `None`. Every one of those failure paths MUST map to `recognized = false` (serialize). An `unwrap_or_default()` or `.unwrap_or(vec![])` anywhere in that plumbing turns "I don't know what this touches" into "this touches nothing" — the exact inversion that causes a fork. Grep the patch for `unwrap_or_default` on any dep-set path before merging.

5. STALE ANALYSIS AFTER PublishModule. The cached `NormalizedReadWriteSetAnalysis` is computed over a module set. A `PublishModule` tx changes that set, so a cached analysis is stale for every tx after it in the same block. Aptos's answer is to not parallelize across a publish. AINCORE already runs PublishModule as an unrecognized singleton batch — keep that, and additionally invalidate/rebuild the cache after the publish commits, before scheduling the next block. Building it mid-block is not safe.

6. NON-DETERMINISM SNEAKING IN THROUGH THE FALLBACK. Whatever re-execution/fallback policy you choose must be a deterministic function of the block contents, identical on every node. "Re-run sequentially if a conflict was detected" is fine because the conflict test is deterministic. "Re-run if the rayon thread pool observed X" or anything depending on thread scheduling, wall-clock, or worker count is a fork generator. This is the same class of bug as BLOCKER-4's local-availability-dependent anchor and blockchain/src/lib.rs:56's `SystemTime::now()` in the header hash — the codebase has a demonstrated pattern of letting local runtime state leak into consensus-visible output, so audit the new code specifically for it.

7. PARALLELISM COLLAPSE, then a panicked rollback. Correct conflict detection will visibly reduce throughput, because the current numbers are partly the product of missing conflicts. Expect the ValidatorSet/SupplyStats hot key to serialize most system txs (pitfall in the plan above). Have the delayed-field/counter-split answer ready BEFORE benchmarking, or the measured regression will create pressure to weaken the conflict test — which is how this bug class comes back.

8. THE READ SET IS NOT OPTIONAL. Skipping the recording resolver and approximating read set := write set is tempting and is wrong in a way that is hard to see in tests: it catches write-write and write-then-read-of-a-written-key, but misses read-here-write-there. `withdraw_unbonded` reading ValidatorSet and writing a CoinStore is exactly that shape.

9. `append_supply_tracker_updates` (lib.rs:975-1010) reads `self.db.get("sys:total_supply")` — the pre-batch value — and mirrors ValidatorSet.total_supply into it. It only fires when the tx wrote `validator_set_key()`, so it is not a universal hot key, but it means two ValidatorSet-writing txs in one batch corrupt the mirror through the same last-write-wins hole. Layer 1 fixes it incidentally; a Layer-0-only patch does not, and the MAX_SUPPLY tripwire at :995 reads the corrupted mirror, so it will keep failing to fire.

10. DON'T PORT SUI'S DECLARED-INPUTS MODEL AS-IS. It is tempting ("just make txs declare their objects") and it is unsound in core Move: without removing `borrow_global_mut`, a declaration is unverifiable and you have rebuilt analyze_tx with extra steps and user-supplied inputs. Sui's guarantee comes from a language restriction AINCORE's VM does not have.

research.how_reference_impls_do_it:
=== Q1. THE EXACT ANCHOR COMMIT RULE, AND WHY IT CANNOT DEPEND ON LOCAL AVAILABILITY ===

The reference protocols never make a *choice* that depends on what the node happens to hold. They make a *three-valued decision* (COMMIT / SKIP / UNDECIDED) about a leader whose identity is fixed in advance by a pure function of (round, committee). Local availability only ever determines WHEN a node reaches a decision, never WHICH decision it reaches.

(a) The leader is fixed, never substituted.
  - narwhal/consensus/src/bullshark.rs, `fn leader()`: `let leader = &committee.leader(round); dag.get(&round).and_then(|x| x.get(leader))`. If that specific authority's certificate is not in the local DAG, `process_certificate` does `None => return Ok(Vec::new())` — do nothing this tick, retry on the next certificate. There is no attempt-2, no backup leader, no scan over other authorities.
  - Mysticeti `BaseCommitter::elect_leader` -> `leader_schedule.elect_leader(round, leader_offset)`; multi-leader/backup-leader configurations exist, but each backup is a *separate BaseCommitter instance with its own fixed leader_offset applied on every node identically*, not a local-availability fallback.

(b) Direct COMMIT: 2f+1 (quorum) stake of certificates/votes.
  - Mysticeti `enough_leader_support(decision_round, leader_block)`: counts blocks at the decision round that are certificates (each certificate itself needs QuorumThreshold of votes among its ancestors) via a `StakeAggregator<QuorumThreshold>`.
  - Bullshark paper Alg.3 L86/L91: `if |{v' in votes : v'.source in steadyVoters[w] AND strong_path(v', v)}| >= 2f+1 then commit_leader(v)`.
  - Old narwhal Bullshark uses the DAG-Rider/Alg.5 form: `stake < committee.validity_threshold()` (= f+1 stake) over round r+1 certs whose `header.parents` contain the leader digest. Tusk (Narwhal paper Sec.5) is also f+1: 'commits the elected leader block b of a wave w if there are f+1 blocks in the second round of w that refer to b'.

(c) Direct SKIP: 2f+1 stake of *blame* (Mysticeti only, and this is the important modern addition).
  - `enough_leader_blame(voting_round=leader.round+1, leader)`: a voting block is a blame iff `voting_block.ancestors().iter().all(|a| a.author != leader)`. 2f+1 stake of blames => `LeaderStatus::Skip`, because a certificate for that leader can then never exist.

(d) Everything else is UNDECIDED, and UNDECIDED BLOCKS THE OUTPUT.
  - `leaders_with_enough_support.pop().unwrap_or(LeaderStatus::Undecided(leader))`.
  - `UniversalCommitter::try_decide` builds the leader list from high round down, then: "The decided sequence is the longest prefix of decided leaders" — `let Some(decided_leader) = leader.into_decided_leader(..) else { break };`. One undecided leader stalls all later commits rather than letting a node run ahead on a different sequence.

(e) The indirect rule is what makes the 2f+1/f+1 gap safe, and it is the formal determinism argument.
  Bullshark paper, §5.2 (verbatim structure): "if some party commits either a fallback or a steady-state leader by seeing 2f+1 votes, then all other parties see at least f+1 of these votes." Hence:
    - direct commit threshold 2f+1  =>  every other honest node necessarily observes >= f+1
    - indirect commit threshold f+1  =>  every other honest node will therefore also commit it
    - skip is only taken when a leader provably has <= f votes, i.e. no one could have committed it.
  Alg.4 L115-120: `if |ssVotes| >= f+1 && |fbVotes| < f+1 { leaderStack.push(v_s) }`, "Otherwise p_i skips the leaders of the current round as it is guaranteed that none of them could have been committed."
  Mysticeti expresses the same thing structurally in `decide_leader_from_anchor`: given a COMMITTED anchor, take `ancestors_at_round(anchor, decision_round)` and Commit the target leader iff one of those is a certificate for it, else Skip. Both the anchor and its ancestor set are identical on every node (the anchor is committed, so its causal history is complete and non-equivocable), therefore the Commit/Skip verdict is identical on every node.
  Narwhal/Tusk paper states the same as Lemma 1 + Lemma 2, and the mechanism is `utils::order_leaders` + `linked(leader, prev_leader, dag)`: past leaders are ordered iff a path exists from the newly committed leader, computed over the committed leader's causal history.

  => The invariant: a node's *local view* can only make it decide LATER. It can never make it decide DIFFERENTLY, because (i) the leader identity is not a function of the DAG, (ii) the thresholds are quorum-intersecting so two honest nodes cannot reach opposite direct verdicts, and (iii) every retroactive verdict is computed relative to an already-committed anchor, whose sub-DAG is byte-identical everywhere.


=== Q2. THE CAUSAL-HISTORY RULE: NEVER PROCESS A VERTEX BEFORE ALL PARENTS ARE LOCAL ===

Answer: never. Causal completeness is an *admission gate*, enforced before the vertex enters the structure the consensus rule reads.

  - Bullshark paper Alg.2 L51-59, `try_add_to_dag(v)`: `if for all v' in v.weakEdges U v.strongEdges : v' in Union_{k>=1} DAG[k] then DAG[v.round] <- DAG[v.round] U {v} ... return true; buffer <- buffer U {v}; return false`. L31-37: on r_deliver, `if not try_add_to_dag(v) then buffer <- buffer U {v}` else drain the buffer and retry every buffered vertex. Paper text §4.2: "a vertex is added to the DAG only if all the vertices it includes as references are already delivered."
  - narwhal core.rs L433-446: `if certificate.round() > self.gc_round + 1 && !self.synchronizer.deliver_certificate(&certificate).await? { ...certificates_suspended... return Ok(()) }`. Note the ordering: the suspension check happens BEFORE `self.certificate_store.write(certificate)` and before `certificates_aggregators.append()`. A cert with missing ancestors is neither stored, nor counted toward round advance, nor shown to consensus.
  - Fetch mechanism, headers: `Synchronizer::get_parents(header)` returns an EMPTY vec if any parent digest is absent and sends `WaiterMessage::SyncParents(missing, header)` to the HeaderWaiter; Core treats the empty vec as "suspended: missing parent(s)".
  - Fetch mechanism, certificates: `Synchronizer::deliver_certificate(cert)` iterates `certificate.header.parents`, and on the first `!has_processed_certificate(digest)` sends the whole cert to `tx_certificate_waiter` and returns false. `CertificateWaiter::waiter` does `try_join_all(missing.map(|x| store.notify_read(x)))` under a `tokio::select!` with a cancel handle (cancelled when the round is GC'd), then loops the certificate back to `tx_core` for reprocessing.
  - Mysticeti `BlockManager::try_accept_one_block`: for every ancestor above gc_round not in `dag_state.contains_blocks(...)`, insert into `missing_ancestors`, record `block_manager_missing_ancestors_by_authority` metric, add to `ancestors_to_fetch`, and return `TryAcceptResult::Suspended(ancestors_to_fetch)`. Suspended blocks live in `suspended_blocks: BTreeMap<BlockRef, SuspendedBlock>` and are released transitively by `try_unsuspend_children_blocks(block_ref)`. The fetch loop is `consensus/core/src/synchronizer.rs` (periodic + on-demand `fetch_blocks` from peers).
  - Consequence exploited downstream: because acceptance is gated, the commit path may *assert* completeness rather than tolerate gaps. `Linearizer::linearize_sub_dag`: `.expect("We should have all uncommitted blocks in dag state.")`. `BaseCommitter::find_supported_block`: `.unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("Block not found in storage: {:?}", ancestor))`. `is_certificate`: `assert!(reference.round <= gc_round, "Block not found in storage ... and is not below gc_round")`. narwhal: `.expect("We should have the whole history by now")` in both the support sum and `linked()`.
    The reference implementations deliberately CRASH on a missing parent during commit. They consider silently continuing to be worse than halting.
  - Availability is also cryptographically guaranteed, which is why fetching always succeeds: Narwhal paper §3.1, "A certificate of availability includes 2f+1 signatures, ie. at least f+1 honest validators have checked and stored the block", and §4.1, on receiving a certificate for round r+1 a validator "can request all blocks in its causal history from validators that signed the certificates".


=== Q3. HOW A NODE ADVANCES ITS OWN ROUND ===

Precondition, stated three ways:
  - Narwhal paper §3.1: "Once certificates for round r-1 are accumulated from 2f+1 distinct validators, a validator moves the local round to r, creates, and broadcasts a block for the new round." Block validity condition 3: "be at round 0 (genesis), or contain certificates for at least 2f+1 blocks of round r-1."
  - Bullshark Alg.2 L61-64: `procedure try_advance_round(): if |DAG[round]| >= 2f+1 then round <- round+1; start timer; wait <- true; broadcast_vertex(round)`.
  - Mysticeti `ThresholdClock::add_block`: `Ordering::Equal => if self.aggregator.add(block.author, committee) { self.round = block.round + 1 }` where the aggregator is `StakeAggregator<QuorumThreshold>`.

What prevents being pushed to a round you cannot build parents for — this is the crux, and all three protocols answer it the same way: **the round jump is derived from the local quorum, never from a remote peer's round number.**
  - Bullshark Alg.2 L53-55: the catch-up jump is `if |DAG[v.round]| >= 2f+1 AND v.round > round then round <- v.round`. The condition is on the *size of the local DAG at that round*, i.e. you jump only to a round for which you already hold a parent quorum. Paper §4.2: "once p_i delivers 2f+1 vertices in a round r > round, p_i jumps forward to round r".
  - narwhal core.rs/proposer.rs: two distinct signals.
      * The weak signal: `let minimal_round_for_parents = certificate.round().saturating_sub(1); tx_proposer.send((vec![], minimal_round_for_parents, epoch))` — a lone certificate at round r only forbids proposing BELOW r-1; it is sent with an EMPTY parent vector and it can never make the proposer emit a header, because `let enough_parents = !self.last_parents.is_empty();` gates `make_header`.
      * The strong signal: only when `certificates_aggregators.entry(round).append(cert, &committee)` returns `Some(parents)` (stake quorum reached) does core send `(parents, certificate.round(), epoch)`; the proposer then does `Ordering::Greater => { self.round = round; self.last_parents = parents; }`. The round and the parents arrive as one atomic pair.
  - Mysticeti `ThresholdClock::add_block`, `Ordering::Greater` branch, with the in-source justification: "If we processed block for round r, we also have stored 2f+1 blocks from r-1". That is sound *only because* BlockManager refuses to accept a block until all its ancestors are present, and a valid block at round r carries 2f+1 ancestors at r-1. Causal-completeness gating (Q2) is what makes fast-forward safe.
  - Additional belt: the proposer's own header always carries `self.last_parents.drain(..)`, so a header cannot be built without the very quorum that authorized the round.


=== Q4. DETERMINISTIC LINEARIZATION OF THE ORDERED SUB-DAG ===

Two stages, both total functions of the (identical) committed sub-DAG.

Stage 1 — sequence of leaders (outer order):
  - narwhal: `order_leaders(...).iter().rev()` — oldest leader first; each is included only via `linked()`.
  - Bullshark Alg.4/Alg.5 `commit_leader(v)`: push v on `leaderStack`, walk `r <- v.round - 2` down while `r > committedRound`, pushing each strongly-linked previous leader, then `order_vertices()` pops the stack (oldest first).
  - Mysticeti: `UniversalCommitter::try_decide` returns leaders in ascending round (built with `push_front` while iterating rounds descending), truncated at the first Undecided.

Stage 2 — flatten each leader's sub-DAG:
  - narwhal `utils::order_dag`: LIFO DFS pre-order from the leader over `x.header.parents`, with `already_ordered: HashSet<CertificateDigest>` and a per-authority high-water skip (`state.last_committed.get(&origin) == Some(&certificate.round())`), then `ordered.retain(|x| x.round() + gc_depth >= state.last_committed_round)` and finally `ordered.sort_by_key(|x| x.round())` (stable sort, so DFS order is the intra-round tiebreak; `parents` is an ordered set of digests, so the DFS itself is deterministic).
  - Mysticeti `Linearizer::linearize_sub_dag`: same LIFO DFS, filtering ancestors by `ancestor.round > gc_round && !dag_state.is_committed(ancestor)`, with `assert!(dag_state.set_committed(&ancestor.reference()))` so a double-commit panics; then the explicit total order in `commit::sort_sub_dag_blocks`:
        blocks.sort_by(|a, b| a.round().cmp(&b.round()).then_with(|| a.author().cmp(&b.author())))
    i.e. **(round ASC, authority-index ASC)** — a full deterministic key, not a hash tiebreak and not DFS-order-dependent.
  - Narwhal paper §5.1: "after ordering a block leader each validator orders the leader's causal history by some pre-define deterministic rule"; combined with the Containment property, "all honest validators agree on the total order of the DAG's blocks."
research.pitfalls:
1. **Deleting the round-robin fallback without adding the back-fill (P1 without P2) converts a fork into a halt.** The fallback loop at ordering.rs:503 is currently the only liveness mechanism when a leader is offline. In the reference stack, liveness under a dead leader comes from (a) the direct-skip rule (2f+1 blame) and (b) the retroactive `order_leaders`/`commit_leader` back-fill, NOT from electing someone else. Land P1 and P2 in the same commit or the chain stops on the first offline validator.

2. **`finalized_round` is currently a one-way ratchet with no skip record — the back-fill must be written to be idempotent against it.** `try_commit` rejects `anchor_round <= self.finalized_round` (:487-491) and sets `finalized_round = max(finalized_round, anchor_round)` (:594). If you add the backward walk but keep advancing `finalized_round` on every direct commit *before* the walk completes, the walk's `while r > self.finalized_round` terminates immediately and back-fills nothing. Compute `to_commit` against the OLD `finalized_round`, then advance it.

3. **`committed_set` is a bounded window (`COMMITTED_SEQ_WINDOW`), not a per-authority high-water mark.** `find_causal_history` prunes with `!self.committed_set.contains(parent)`, and `record_committed` drains the oldest entries. Once P2 makes the causal walk reach further back (across skipped rounds), an evicted-but-committed vertex will be re-walked and re-emitted — a duplicate execution. narwhal solves this with `state.last_committed: HashMap<AuthorityId, Round>` plus a gc_depth retain; Mysticeti with `dag_state.set_committed()` + `assert!` on double-commit. Switch to a per-author `last_committed_round` map (and keep `gc_round` as the hard floor) before widening the walk, or you will trade a fork for a replay.

4. **A hard causal-completeness gate is a liveness cliff if the fetcher is missing or asymmetric.** Once `add_vertex` suspends on missing parents, a node with no working `REQ_VERTEX` path silently stops accepting everything and looks alive (it still gossips its own vertices) while contributing nothing. Narwhal pairs the gate with CertificateWaiter + a store `notify_read` + a cancel handle tied to GC; Mysticeti pairs it with a periodic `synchronizer.rs` fetch loop and a `block_manager_missing_ancestors_by_authority` metric. Ship the fetcher, the GC-driven cancellation (drop pending vertices below `finalized_round - 10`), and a metric/log for suspended-vertex count in the same change — otherwise the first packet loss wedges a node in a way that is invisible.

5. **`assert!`/`expect` on missing blocks is correct in the reference impls only because acceptance is gated — do not copy the panics first.** `linearize_sub_dag`'s `.expect("We should have all uncommitted blocks in dag state.")` and `find_supported_block`'s `panic!` are load-bearing invariant checks downstream of BlockManager. If you add those assertions to AINCORE before P4 lands, every node crashes on the first out-of-order gossip. Order: gate + fetcher first, then convert `find_causal_history`'s silent skip to `Err`, and only then consider hardening to a panic.

6. **The round fast-forward off-by-one is a real bootstrap hazard, and dag.rs:809-816 already carries a scar from it.** The current comment documents a multi-machine bootstrap deadlock fixed by using `>` rather than `>=`. Setting `current_round = vertex.round + 1` on a bare remote vertex is the *other* half of that same bug. If you change it to `target + 1` gated on a local quorum, re-test the 3-machine cold-start specifically: with n=3 and >2/3 stake quorum you need all 3 present, so a node that jumps to `target+1` on a 2-of-3 view will stall. Verify `stake_quorum_met` semantics at the exact validator count you launch with, and consider that this defect and the n>=4 mainnet blocker interact.

7. **Leader election is still proposer-biasable, and P1 makes that matter more.** The in-code comment at ordering.rs:~695 flags audit H-2: `step1_beacon` is a VDF over `anchor_round + finality_digest`, and the anchor proposer can bias its content. With the fallback removed, a biased beacon no longer just changes which of several reachable leaders wins — it becomes the single point that determines the anchor. Determinism (every node computes the same leader) is preserved and that is what fixes the fork; unpredictability is not, so leader-grinding/censorship remains open. Do not let "we fixed BLOCKER-4" be read as "leader election is sound."

8. **Do not port Bullshark's steady-state/fallback two-leader wave machinery.** Alg.3's `steadyVoters`/`fallbackVoters` vote-typing exists to let the asynchronous fallback path coexist with the synchronous fast path, and it is where the 2f+1-vs-f+1 subtleties bite. AINCORE has a single leader per anchor round; the eventually-synchronous Bullshark (paper Alg.5, ~200 LOC, the version Mysten actually productionized) is the right target and it has no fallback leaders at all. Porting the wave/vote-type logic partially is far more dangerous than not porting it.

9. **Determinism of the sort key is not enough if the input set differs.** ordering.rs:775-790 already sorts by (round, hash); the fork does not come from the tiebreak, it comes from `sequence` containing different vertices on different nodes. Fixing the comparator alone (a tempting small diff) changes nothing. The fix must be at the set level: same anchor (P1/P2), same causal history (P3/P4).

10. **BLOCKER-4 is masked in testing exactly where you will test it.** The audit notes only 2 of 349k rounds carried transactions, so blocks were byte-identical regardless of ordering. Any regression test that mines empty blocks will pass with all of these bugs still present. The acceptance test must be: n>=4 nodes, non-empty payloads every round, one node artificially delayed or dropping a fraction of gossip, then assert byte-equality of `sys:state_root` and the full committed-hash sequence across nodes for several hundred rounds — not just equal heights.

research.topic: Deterministic block headers and time in BFT chains — how production chains make the header a pure function of committed data, and the corrected design for AINCORE (consensus/blockchain/src/lib.rs:56 SystemTime::now() inside the header constructor)

sources.title: CometBFT — BFT Time specification (spec/consensus/bft-time.md)
sources.key_takeaway: Block.Time for height H is computed by MedianTime over the Timestamp fields of the Precommit messages in LastCommit (the commit set for H-1), weighted by validator voting power. It is a deterministic pure function of data already inside the block — every node recomputes the identical value from LastCommit; nobody reads a local clock at header-construction time. The precommit-side rule that feeds it is Timestamp = max(now, LockedBlock.Time + 1ms) (or ProposalBlock.Time + 1ms, else now) — the +1ms tick is what guarantees strict monotonicity. Because the median is stake-weighted and >2/3 voting power is honest, the selected value is always some honest validator's timestamp, so <1/3 Byzantine stake cannot move it up or down arbitrarily.

sources.title: CometBFT — Proposer-Based Timestamps (PBTS), v1.x replacement for BFT Time
sources.key_takeaway: PBTS flips to a single AUTHOR-SET timestamp: the proposer stamps its local clock, and the value is then *validated* by every other node against a timeliness predicate (within PRECISION + MSGDELAY of the receiving validator's clock at proposal-receipt time). The validation is a VOTE-time admission rule, not a header-recomputation rule — once committed, the header value is fixed and replicated verbatim. Requires NTP-synced validator clocks; a proposer whose clock is out of bounds simply loses its block (liveness cost, not safety cost).

sources.title: Aptos — aptos-framework timestamp.move (update_global_time)
sources.key_takeaway: The on-chain clock is a resource `CurrentTimeMicroseconds { microseconds: u64 }` written by the VM-privileged `update_global_time(vm, proposer, timestamp)` executed as the BlockMetadata transaction at the head of every block. Two paths: proposer == @vm_reserved (NIL block) asserts `now == timestamp` (clock frozen); otherwise asserts `now < timestamp` (STRICTLY increasing) before writing. So the chain's notion of time is a committed state value advanced by an ordinary state transition — replay-deterministic by construction, and any Move contract reading time reads this resource, never a host clock.

sources.title: Aptos — consensus-types Block::verify_well_formed
sources.key_takeaway: Three separate bounds, and the split between them is the important part: (1) NIL / reconfig-suffix blocks must have EXACTLY the parent's timestamp; (2) normal blocks must have strictly increasing timestamps vs parent — both are pure functions of committed data and hold at replay; (3) 'Blocks must not be too far in the future' — non-NIL blocks may not exceed local now + 300s. Rule (3) is a local-clock rule and it is deliberately applied only on the *proposal-receipt* path, not on state-sync/replay, because a local-clock predicate is not a deterministic validity rule.

sources.title: Sui / Mysticeti — consensus/core/src/linearizer.rs (calculate_commit_timestamp)
sources.key_takeaway: The committed sub-DAG's timestamp (which becomes CheckpointSummary.timestamp_ms) is NOT the leader block's own timestamp. `calculate_commit_timestamp` selects the leader's parent blocks (round leader.round()-1), calls `median_timestamp_by_stake` — `median_timestamps_by_stake_inner` sorts the timestamps and walks cumulative stake, returning the first ts where `cumulative_stake > total_stake / 2` — then applies `timestamp_ms.max(last_commit_timestamp_ms)` so commit timestamps are monotonic even if the median regresses. This is the exact DAG-native analogue of CometBFT's MedianTime and the closest structural match to AINCORE's anchor-commit model.

sources.title: Ethereum consensus specs — compute_timestamp_at_slot / process_execution_payload
sources.key_takeaway: Ethereum PoS removes proposer discretion entirely: `compute_timestamp_at_slot(state, slot) = genesis_time + (slot - GENESIS_SLOT) * SECONDS_PER_SLOT`, and `process_execution_payload` asserts `payload.timestamp == compute_timestamp_at_slot(...)`. The timestamp carries zero entropy — it is a pure function of the slot number, explicitly so that proposers cannot manipulate execution-layer time for contracts that depend on it. This is the strongest possible anti-grinding design and is only available to chains with fixed slots.

sources.title: AINCORE — consensus/blockchain/src/lib.rs (the bug)
sources.key_takeaway: `Block::new_with_roots` calls SystemTime::now() at :56 and `calculate_header_hash` folds `header.timestamp` into the preimage at :104. Sole call site is dag.rs:911, which every validator runs independently after committing the same anchor — so each node derives a different header.hash for byte-identical block content. That hash becomes `self.latest_block_hash` (dag.rs:919) and the next block's `prev_hash`, and is appended to the accumulator. `calculate_header_hash` also has a legacy conditional at :98 (`if !state_root.is_empty() || !receipts_root.is_empty()`) that makes the preimage SHAPE depend on data — a second determinism landmine.

sources.title: AINCORE — sync/src/lib.rs local-clock validity rule on replayed blocks
sources.key_takeaway: :264 rejects any peer block whose `prev_hash` != local latest hash — so once two nodes derive different header hashes at the same height, sync is permanently wedged, not merely divergent. :287-297 applies `block.header.timestamp > now + 30` to blocks being REPLAYED from a peer — exactly the anti-pattern Aptos avoids: a local-clock predicate used as a validity rule on historical data. A node with a lagging clock, or one syncing a chain whose clock ran ahead, rejects valid history.

sources.title: AINCORE — core/vm_move/stdlib/sources/epoch.move (the part that is already right)
sources.key_takeaway: `epoch::now_seconds()` returns `epoch_start_time`, a monotonic virtual-second accumulator advanced only by `advance_epoch`. It is a committed state value, not a host clock — structurally the same choice as Aptos's CurrentTimeMicroseconds. delegation.move:249/263/344/356 (unbonding + commission-change deadlines) read it. So AINCORE currently has NO in-VM wall-clock dependency; the corrected header design must preserve that separation rather than wiring the header timestamp into the VM.

Must be redirected to `epoch::now_seconds()` / the committed header timestamp before that TODO is implemented.

research.how_reference_impls_do_it:
ANSWERING (a) IS THE TIMESTAMP AUTHOR-SET AND REPLICATED, NEVER LOCALLY RECOMPUTED?

Universally yes — no production BFT chain recomputes a header timestamp from a local clock at commit time. What differs is only WHO sets it, and all four designs make it a pure function of data already inside the committed block:

- CometBFT BFT Time (legacy, still on most Cosmos chains): the value is DERIVED, not stamped. `Block.Time` at height H = `MedianTime(LastCommit)` — the stake-weighted median of the `Timestamp` fields of the Precommit messages that formed the commit for H-1. LastCommit is embedded in the block, so every node recomputes bit-identically; the "clock read" happened earlier, at precommit time, and was signed and replicated. The precommit rule is `Timestamp = max(now, LockedBlock.Time + 1ms)`, falling back to `max(now, ProposalBlock.Time + 1ms)`, else `now`.
- CometBFT PBTS (v1.x, recommended for new chains): the proposer stamps its own clock into the proposal. Every other validator checks a timeliness predicate at PROPOSAL-RECEIPT time (within PRECISION + MSGDELAY of its own clock) and votes nil if it fails. Once committed, the value is replicated verbatim forever. Validation is at vote time; it is never re-derived.
- Aptos: the proposer's timestamp rides in the block, and it is applied to state by `timestamp::update_global_time(vm, proposer, timestamp)` inside the BlockMetadata transaction that is prepended to every block. The chain's clock is therefore a Move resource `CurrentTimeMicroseconds { microseconds }` mutated by an ordinary, replayable state transition.
- Sui/Mysticeti: DERIVED like CometBFT, but DAG-native. `Linearizer::calculate_commit_timestamp` takes the committed leader, selects its parent blocks at round `leader.round() - 1`, and calls `median_timestamp_by_stake`; `median_timestamps_by_stake_inner` sorts the parents' timestamps and accumulates stake, returning the first ts where `cumulative_stake > total_stake / 2`. It then returns `timestamp_ms.max(last_commit_timestamp_ms)`. That value becomes `CommittedSubDag.timestamp_ms` and flows into `CheckpointSummary.timestamp_ms`.
- Ethereum PoS: zero author discretion. `compute_timestamp_at_slot(state, slot) = state.genesis_time + (slot - GENESIS_SLOT) * SECONDS_PER_SLOT`, and `process_execution_payload` asserts `payload.timestamp == compute_timestamp_at_slot(state, state.slot)`.

(b) WHAT VALIDITY BOUNDS ARE ENFORCED

The load-bearing insight is that every chain enforces TWO DISJOINT CLASSES of rule, and never confuses them:

CLASS B — deterministic validity (pure function of committed data; enforced by everyone, including at replay/state-sync; part of what makes the header verifiable forever):
- Strict monotonicity vs parent. Aptos `Block::verify_well_formed`: "Blocks must have strictly increasing timestamps" for normal blocks; NIL / reconfig-suffix blocks must have EXACTLY the parent's timestamp ("Nil/reconfig suffix block must have same timestamp as parent"). Mirrored in `update_global_time`: `assert!(now < timestamp)` for a real proposer, `assert!(now == timestamp)` when `proposer == @vm_reserved`.
- Non-decreasing commit timestamps. Sui: `timestamp_ms.max(last_commit_timestamp_ms)` — it clamps rather than rejects, so a regressing median cannot stall the commit path.
- The +1 tick that manufactures strictness. CometBFT precommits use `parent.Time + 1ms` as a floor so the derived median for the next height cannot equal the previous one.
- Exact-equality to a derived value. Ethereum: `payload.timestamp == compute_timestamp_at_slot(...)`.

CLASS A — local-clock admission (a liveness/spam filter, NOT a validity rule; applied only when a proposal/vertex first arrives over gossip, deliberately NOT applied at replay):
- Aptos: "Blocks must not be too far in the future" — now + 300s, non-NIL blocks only, checked in the proposal path. State sync replaying committed history does not apply it.
- CometBFT PBTS: the timeliness predicate (PRECISION + MSGDELAY) is evaluated only when deciding how to vote on a proposal. Chains that adopt PBTS are told to keep validators NTP-synced; a proposer outside the window loses its block, which is a liveness cost, never a safety cost.

(c) GRINDING PROTECTION, AND WHAT DEPENDS ON THE TIMESTAMP

- Ethereum eliminates grinding by construction: the timestamp carries zero entropy, explicitly so proposers cannot manipulate execution-layer time for time-dependent contracts.
- CometBFT and Sui eliminate SINGLE-PARTY control via the stake-weighted median: because >2/3 of stake is honest, the selected value is always some honest validator's timestamp, so Byzantine stake below 1/3 cannot push the value up or down at will. This is the whole reason both chose a median over "the leader's own clock".
- Aptos accepts proposer discretion but fences it: bounded above by now+300s at admission, bounded below by strict monotonicity forever, and any consumer must read the committed `CurrentTimeMicroseconds` resource rather than a host clock.
- What depends on it, in all of them: it is the ONLY time source available to smart contracts (Aptos `timestamp::now_seconds`, Cosmos `ctx.BlockTime()`, Solidity `block.timestamp`), which is why vesting, unbonding, auction and oracle-staleness logic is safe against node-clock skew. Notably, none of them derive consensus randomness or leader election from the timestamp — that would hand the proposer a free grinding dimension.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX FOR AINCORE: adopt Sui's model (it is the same DAG-anchor-commit architecture), staged so that step 1 is safe to land before BLOCKER-3/4 are fixed and step 4 is the grinding-resistant end state.

STEP 0 — make the constructor pure (mechanical, no policy change)
In /Users/macbookpro/Documents/AINCORE-Blockchain/consensus/blockchain/src/lib.rs, delete the `SystemTime::now()` at :56 and make `timestamp: u64` an explicit parameter of `new_with_roots` (and of `new`, which forwards). Delete `use std::time::{SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH}` from the file entirely so re-introducing ambient time is a visible diff in review. The constructor then has one job: hash the fields it was given. Do the same at :126 for `Vertex::new` (dag.rs:429 already stamps the vertex timestamp inline at the author, which is the correct place — an author-set clock read is fine; a commit-time clock read is not).

While in the file, fix the second determinism landmine at :98: `calculate_header_hash` changes its PREIMAGE SHAPE based on whether state_root/receipts_root are empty. Replace with an explicit `version: u8` in the header, folded into the preimage as a fixed-width byte, with v0 = legacy layout and v1 = always-include-roots. A preimage whose field set depends on field values is a fork waiting for the first empty-root edge case.

STEP 1 — v1 timestamp source: the anchor vertex, clamped (land this now)
At dag.rs:911, the block is already built from a specific committed anchor. Every node that commits height H has that anchor vertex by definition, it is Ed25519-signed by its author, its timestamp is already bound into `vertex.calculate_hash()` (verified at dag.rs:705 via the PWN-001 recompute check), and its value is already drift-checked at dag.rs:659-676. So it is exactly the "author-set and replicated" value the reference chains use.

Add to consensus/blockchain (so sync can call the identical function):

    pub const MAX_BLOCK_TS_DELTA_SECS: u64 = 300;

    /// Pure function of committed data. Same inputs -> same output on every
    /// node, at first execution and at replay. No ambient clock.
    pub fn derive_block_timestamp(anchor_ts: u64, parent_ts: u64) -> u64 {
        anchor_ts
            .max(parent_ts.saturating_add(1))                      // Aptos: strictly increasing
            .min(parent_ts.saturating_add(MAX_BLOCK_TS_DELTA_SECS)) // bound runaway
    }

Order matters: `.max` then `.min`, and MAX_BLOCK_TS_DELTA_SECS >= 1 so the two clamps can never invert. Genesis (height 1) uses the genesis timestamp from genesis.json as `parent_ts`.

Call it at dag.rs:911 with `anchor_vertex.timestamp` and `parent_header.timestamp`, and pass the result into `Block::new_with_roots`. Persist the anchor used, `block_anchor:{height} -> anchor_vertex_hash`, so a replaying node can prove which anchor produced the header without re-running leader election.

HARD DEPENDENCY, state it in the plan: this makes the header a pure function of (anchor vertex, parent header, txs, state_root, receipts_root). Fix ordering BEFORE or WITH this, or you have converted "different timestamp" into "different anchor", same fork.

Class B, deterministic, enforced everywhere including replay and inside the block-validity function shared by dag.rs and sync:
  - `header.timestamp > parent.timestamp` (strict, Aptos)
  - `header.timestamp - parent.timestamp <= MAX_BLOCK_TS_DELTA_SECS`
  - `header.timestamp == derive_block_timestamp(anchor.timestamp, parent.timestamp)` where the anchor is available — the Ethereum-style exact-equality check, the strongest form
  - vertex causal monotonicity, in dag.rs `add_vertex`: `vertex.timestamp >= max(p.timestamp for p in parents present in the DAG)`. Deterministic, because parents are committed DAG data.
Class A, local clock, gossip-admission ONLY:
  - keep dag.rs:659-676 (`vertex.timestamp <= now + 30`) exactly where it is
  - DELETE sync/src/lib.rs:287-297. That check applies a local-clock predicate to REPLAYED history and is the Aptos anti-pattern verbatim. A node with a lagging clock, or one syncing a chain whose committed timestamps ran ahead, rejects valid finalized blocks — and because sync/src/lib.rs:264 rejects on `prev_hash` mismatch, a single such rejection wedges that node permanently rather than degrading gracefully.

STEP 3 — author-side proposal rule (the +1 tick)
In dag.rs at vertex construction (:429), replace the bare clock read with the CometBFT precommit rule:
  `timestamp = max(local_now, max(parent_vertex.timestamp for parent in parents) + 1)`
This makes vertex timestamps monotone along every DAG path, so the Class-B causal check above can never reject an honest proposer, and it guarantees the anchor timestamp already exceeds its own causal history before any clamping.

STEP 4 — v2, remove single-proposer control (land once BLOCKER-4's causal-completeness gate exists)
Replace `anchor_ts` with Sui's stake-weighted median over the anchor's PARENT set:

    fn median_timestamp_by_stake(parents: &[(String /*author*/, u64 /*ts*/)],
                                 validators: &[(String, u64 /*stake*/)]) -> u64 {
        // sort by ts asc; walk cumulative stake; return first ts where
        // cumulative_stake > total_stake / 2
    }
    let ts = derive_block_timestamp(median_timestamp_by_stake(...), parent_ts);

This is only safe after BLOCKER-4's fix, because it requires the full parent set to be present locally — which is exactly what the causal-completeness gate (defer the commit and fetch missing vertices instead of silently skipping at ordering.rs:755-772) provides. With <1/3 Byzantine stake the median is always some honest validator's value, so no single anchor author picks the chain's clock. Sort the parents canonically (by author address) before the walk, and require the parent quorum that dag.rs:360-379 already computes, so the input multiset is identical on every node.

STEP 5 — restart/replay determinism, enforced by test
Add a test that walks storage from height 1 to latest, reconstructs each header from (stored parent header, stored anchor vertex via `block_anchor:{h}`, stored txs, stored roots), and asserts the recomputed `calculate_header_hash` equals the stored `header.hash`. That test is the actual regression guard — it fails the moment anyone reintroduces ambient input into the header, and it is the thing to run after a node restart to prove the chain is replayable. Complement it with a two-engine test in the style of ordering.rs's existing `beacon_is_deterministic_and_history_dependent`: two independently constructed nodes fed the same anchor + parent must produce byte-identical headers.

STEP 6 — keep the VM clock separate, and defuse the two landmines
Do NOT wire the header timestamp into the Move VM. `epoch::now_seconds()` (core/vm_move/stdlib/sources/epoch.move:54) is already a committed monotonic accumulator and is the correct on-chain clock — this is the same architectural choice as Aptos's `CurrentTimeMicroseconds`, and delegation.move's unbonding deadlines depend on it. Off the consensus path today only because on-chain governance execution is still manual (per CLAUDE.md). The moment execution becomes a transaction, that comparison must read the committed clock.
