sequenced_plan.title: Block header determinism — remove SystemTime::now() from the header hash
sequenced_plan.why_this_order: Blocking prerequisite for Steps 7, 9, 11 and 12. new_with_roots calls SystemTime::now() inside the constructor and folds the result into the header hash; the sole call site is dag.rs:911, so today two honest nodes committing byte-identical content derive different block hashes. Until that is fixed you cannot verify a synced block against a peer's, cannot detect a B4 fork, and cannot state a burn-in criterion of 'identical block hash at every height'. Fix: take the timestamp from a deterministic, consensus-agreed source — the anchor vertex's timestamp (already replicated and signed) — and pass it in as a parameter rather than reading the local clock. Median-of-parents is the standard alternative (Tendermint BFT Time / Bitcoin's median-time-past); the anchor timestamp is simpler here because the anchor is already the single ordering authority.

Test: two Executor+DAG instances built from the same genesis, fed the same vertex stream in DIFFERENT arrival orders, produce identical header.hash at every height. On a 2-node local cluster under load, tools/state-diff reports zero block_hash divergence over 1000 blocks.

sequenced_plan.title: Sync — verify execution roots BEFORE committing an unauthenticated peer block
sequenced_plan.why_this_order: Depends on Step 6 (verification is meaningless while header hashes are node-local) and on Step 1 (the write set an aborted tx produces changes, so the roots being compared change). Confirmed by reading the code: sync/src/lib.rs:974 calls execute_block_parallel, which writes the WriteBatch and updates sys:state_root at executor lib.rs:1631-1637 — the commit is INSIDE execution — and only then, at :976, does verify_execution_roots run. A malicious peer's block is therefore applied to local state before it is checked. Fix: give the executor a dry-run mode that returns (updates, roots) without touching RocksDB, verify the roots against the block header, and only then commit — the same order Aptos and Sui use, where the write set is produced, validated against the block, and committed as one gated step.

Second test: a well-formed peer block still applies and advances height. Verified on the live path, not just in unit tests — a 3-node run where one node is fed a forged block from a script and keeps producing blocks.

sequenced_plan.title: B3 — derive current_round from parent-quorum availability, never from a single remote vertex
sequenced_plan.why_this_order: Liveness before safety: a wedged chain cannot produce the payload-carrying blocks that Step 9's determinism gate must be tested against. The bug is confirmed — dag.rs:816-820 sets current_round = vertex.round + 1 from one remote vertex and persists it as latest_proposed_round, while try_create_vertex (:331-338) draws parents only from current_round - 1 and gates on stake-weighted parent quorum (:346-379). One vertex a single round ahead moves the node to a round whose predecessor can never reach quorum, and try_create_vertex stops forever, persisted across restarts. MAX_ROUND_JUMP=10000 (:632) is irrelevant because a jump of 1 does it. No Byzantine intent needed: a validator with a fast ticker suffices. The correct rule is Narwhal's (Danezis, Kokoris-Kogias, Sonnino, Spiegelman, EuroSys 2022) and DAG-Rider's: a validator advances to round r+1 only upon collecting 2f+1 certificates for round r — availability of quorum drives the round, never a peer's claim. Recompute current_round on ingest as (highest round whose round_index holds stake quorum) + 1, monotonic non-decreasing; genuine amnesia recovery then flows through the sync path, not through a round jump.
sequenced_plan.done_when: test_b3_fast_ticker_peer_cannot_wedge: a 4-node harness where node D's ticker runs 5x fast; after 500 rounds all four nodes are still producing vertices and the committed height gap between fastest and slowest is bounded (<10). test_b3_round_never_exceeds_quorum_plus_one: property test over randomized vertex arrival orders asserting current_round <= (max round with stake quorum) + 1 always. test_b3_restart_recovers: kill a node mid-run, restart, confirm it rejoins and resumes proposing within 30 seconds without manual intervention (the persisted latest_proposed_round no longer strands it). Long-partition recovery still works: isolate a node for 200 rounds, reconnect, confirm it catches up via sync.

sequenced_plan.title: B4 — deterministic anchor selection, causal-completeness gate, and vertex fetch
sequenced_plan.why_this_order: Last of the four because it needs Step 6 (comparable block hashes), Step 8 (a chain that keeps running) and Step 2 (non-empty payloads) to be testable at all — it is empirically invisible today only because in 349k rounds just 2 blocks carried transactions, so every node produced identical empty block bytes regardless of ordering. The DEX is exactly what makes payloads non-empty. Three confirmed defects, three fixes. (a) ordering.rs:493-510 loops attempt in 0..max_attempts over get_leader_with_fallback and takes whichever leader vertex happens to be in the LOCAL dag — local availability decides the anchor. Bullshark/DAG-Rider instead fix the anchor by round and leader schedule alone: if the anchor is absent or lacks f+1 support in the following round, the round is SKIPPED and committed indirectly later via a future anchor's causal history — never substituted by a locally-available alternative. (b) find_causal_history (:752-770) walks parents and simply drops any hash not in the local dag, so two nodes with different arrival states commit different tx sets under the same anchor. Fix: if any parent in the causal closure is missing, DEFER the commit — do not commit a partial history. (c) That defer is only safe with a fetch path, which does not exist: add request/response for a vertex by hash over the existing transport (chain_sync::handle_message per the repo's unified-serving convention), matching Narwhal's rule that a certificate is not accepted until its full causal history is stored locally. Also make the VDF leader seed a function of committed state, not local timing.

(c) test_b4_vertex_fetch_round_trip on a live 2-node pair: drop a vertex on the wire, confirm the receiving node requests and receives it and commits without divergence. (d) Live proof: 4 nodes under Step 2's load at >=50 TPS with 10% artificial packet loss for 6 hours, tools/state-diff reports ZERO block_hash or state_root divergence at any height.

sequenced_plan.title: Operational hardening — systemd, n>=4 validators, divergence alerting

Two known mainnet blockers live here: there is no auto-start, so a single reboot froze the 3-node chain for 10 days; and n=3 gives f=0 — a single validator failure halts the chain, so BFT requires n>=4. Neither is a code defect, and neither is discoverable by testing on one machine.

plan.fresh_genesis_required:
YES — exactly once, at Step 11, immediately before burn-in begins.

Which steps force it: Step 1 changes the write set of every aborted transaction, hence sys:state_root and every receipt hash. Step 3 changes compiled stdlib module bytes. Steps 4 and 5 change which writes survive a batch. Step 6 changes the block header hash preimage. Any of these alone makes old and new binaries fork on the first affected block, so a rolling upgrade is not an option under any circumstances — the only two valid paths are a fresh genesis or a coordinated full stop, upgrade all machines, restart.

Cost of a fresh genesis here is essentially zero and this is the decisive fact: the audit established that in 349k rounds only 2 blocks carried transactions at all, and mainnet has not launched. There is no meaningful transaction history to preserve, so preferring a fresh genesis over a stop-and-restart is strictly safer at no cost — it also guarantees no residue of the pre-fix state transition (partially-committed aborted writes, a bricked DEX pool, a corrupted ValidatorSet blob) survives into the chain being burned in.

Sequencing detail: do NOT regenerate genesis after Step 1 and again after Step 6. Land Steps 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 on the branch, ship them as one binary, then cut ONE genesis at Step 11. Every step's intermediate verification runs on local throwaway datadirs, which cost nothing to recreate.

A SECOND genesis is required only if any state-transition or header change lands after the Step 11 burn-in clock starts. If a fix is needed mid-burn-in, the correct response is: land it, cut a new genesis, restart the 72h clock from zero. Do not carry a burn-in result forward across a state-transition change.

Per CLAUDE.md rule 1, regenerating genesis.json needs explicit founder confirmation at that moment — it is not implied by approving this plan.

plan.biggest_risks:
1. THE PAYLOAD PATH HAS NEVER RUN. 2 non-empty blocks in 349k rounds, and bench-tps/src/main.rs:62 still emits a legacy string payload the BCS-only mempool rejects — so nothing in the DEX, delegation, token_factory or staking entry paths has meaningful production hours. Expect Step 11 to surface NEW bugs unrelated to the four blockers. Mitigation: Step 2 is a hard gate, and the burn-in criteria demand >=20% deliberately-aborting transactions so failure paths get exercised at scale, not just happy paths. Budget for a burn-in restart.

2. STEP 9 IS THE SCHEDULE RISK. Deterministic anchoring plus a causal-completeness gate plus a brand-new vertex-fetch path is the only step that adds protocol surface rather than fixing existing code. The completeness gate can deadlock if the fetch path is unreliable (defer forever waiting on a parent nobody serves). Mitigation: build the fetch path FIRST and prove the round trip on live nodes before turning on the defer behaviour; add a bounded retry with a metric so a stalled fetch is loud rather than a silent halt; keep the fetch serving in chain_sync::handle_message per the repo's unified-serving convention rather than adding a second serving path.

3. FIXING B1 WITHOUT FIXING B2 CREATES A NEW CONFLICT. The staged prologue means EVERY transaction now provably writes resource_{payer}_CoinStore, a key that many analyze_tx branches do not declare. Shipping Step 1 alone would increase, not decrease, the odds of a scheduler-induced state-root fork. Mitigation: Steps 1 and 4 must reach mainnet together; they may land as separate commits but must never be separated by a genesis or a burn-in boundary.

4. THE 'IT LOOKS RIGHT' FAILURE MODE. This repo has shipped two fixes that were correct as functions but never executed on the live path. All four blockers survived 16 hardening commits. Mitigation: every "done when" above is stated as an executed observation (a PoC that now fails, a counter that is non-zero, a divergence tool reporting zero over N blocks), not as code review or a passing unit test alone. Step 12 re-runs the original PoCs against the actual burn-in binary.

5. THE OVERLAY'S DELETE ARM. `overlay.get(k).unwrap_or_else(|| base.get(k))` silently resurrects any resource deleted in an earlier stage — one line, silently exploitable, and structurally identical to B2's unbonding-entry exploit. Mitigation: `Some(None) => Ok(None)` is an explicit arm with a dedicated test (test_overlay_staged_delete_is_a_hit_not_a_miss), and the overlay must cover modules as well as resources, with flush_loader_cache_if_invalidated() called after any stage that published — the Loader cache lives on MoveVM, not Session, and is the one piece of state layering does not isolate.

6. A METERED EPILOGUE WOULD REINTRODUCE FREE ABORTS. Stage 3 is empty today only because gas is a flat up-front burn. If a refund model is ever wired onto the shared, near-exhausted meter, an abort consuming the full gas_limit makes the fee write itself run out of gas and vanish — the exact spam vector the whole design protects against. Mitigation: the stage-3 seam exists from day one with a comment stating it must be unmetered plus asserted, mirroring Aptos running its abort hook with &mut UnmeteredGasMeter and then verifying the charge landed.

7. OPERATIONAL, NOT TECHNICAL. n=3 gives f=0, and there is no auto-start — one reboot froze the chain for 10 days. Neither is visible in any test suite. Mitigation: Step 10 is a gate, and the burn-in criteria include unannounced reboots of every machine.

8. EVENTS ARE A LATENT ORACLE-POISONING VECTOR. finish() returns (ChangeSet, Vec<Event>) and AINCORE discards events today. When they are wired to the API/indexer, an aborted stage's events must die with its writes — Sui's drop_writes explicitly clears events for this reason. Mitigation: capture events per stage from the start so it cannot be forgotten later.

9. RESIDUAL, OUT OF SCOPE, TICKET IT: governance.move:114-118 lets a new vote overwrite escrow.proposal_id on a merged escrow, so an old proposal's locked stake becomes claimable on the new proposal's execution. Not a B1 instance and not on the mainnet-blocker path, but it is a real fund-flow bug.
